passage:
Subject: honestly thinking of quitting

Hi Irfan,
It's 1 a.m. and my code still won't run. The same error, three nights in a row. I nearly threw my charger across the hostel room.
You remember Nikhil from our batch? He finished the whole sorting assignment in one evening and then helped four people. Four. I watched him type like the screen was talking to him, and I just sat there feeling thick.
Everyone keeps saying the second semester is where it clicks. For whom? Not for me, clearly.
I'm seriously thinking of switching to the commerce electives next term. At least there I won't feel like the slowest person in every lab.
Don't tell me to 'just keep going'. I know you will. I just needed to say it to someone who won't laugh.

Abhinav

qa.q: How many nights in a row has Abhinav seen the same error?
qa.a: Abhinav has seen the same error three nights in a row.

qa.q: How does Abhinav feel when comparing themself with Nikhil?
qa.a: Abhinav feels slow and thick next to Nikhil, and the comparison turns irritation into a wish to give up.

qa.q: What small step at this stage could help Abhinav before deciding to switch?
qa.a: Abhinav could wait until they are rested, then ask a lab assistant or Nikhil to look at that one error, instead of judging their future at 1 a.m.

qa.q: If you were Irfan reading this email, what would you want to do?
qa.a: I would want to listen first rather than lecture, since Abhinav asked not to be told to 'just keep going', and maybe ask what part feels hardest.

grounding: It shows a learner irritated, comparing themself with a fast classmate and thinking of dropping the skill at the moment it feels hardest to see past.

passage:
Alka, you want the honest version? Fine. Yesterday, at the college pool, a boy of maybe eleven swam past me like a fish. I was holding the rail, coughing, because I had swallowed half the lane again. Four months, Alka. Four months of Tuesday and Friday classes, and I still can't breathe on the side without panicking. The coach keeps saying 'relax your neck'. Relax. As if I'm doing it on purpose.
And the girls from the evening batch, they started after me and they're doing full lengths now. I stood in the shower afterwards and thought, Bhupen, why are you even paying for this? I'm twenty-one. Maybe some people are just not water people.
I haven't cancelled. Not yet. But the form is sitting in my bag, and every time I see it, it looks easier than going back on Friday.

qa.q: How long has Bhupen been taking swimming classes?
qa.a: Bhupen has been taking Tuesday and Friday classes for four months.

qa.q: What does Bhupen's comment 'As if I'm doing it on purpose' suggest about Bhupen's mood?
qa.a: It suggests irritation, both at the coach's advice and at Bhupen's own body, as if the struggle feels unfair and personal.

qa.q: What could help Bhupen at this stage instead of filling in the cancellation form?
qa.a: Bhupen could ask the coach for one small drill to practise just the side breathing, so the next class has a clear, reachable target.

qa.q: How might Alka be affected while listening to this?
qa.a: Alka may feel worried that Bhupen is about to quit, and unsure whether to cheer Bhupen on or simply let the frustration be heard.

grounding: It shows a learner irritated, comparing themself with faster learners and close to dropping the skill, with the quitting urge hard to see past.

passage:
Honestly, Hemant, I'm this close to dropping Japanese. You asked why I've been snapping at everyone. This is why.
Four months of kanji cards, and yesterday in class I blanked on a word I've written fifty times. Fifty! Then the girl next to me, who joined in August, reads the whole paragraph like it's nothing. The teacher smiled at her. I wanted to throw my notebook out of the window.
I keep doing maths in my head. If she got there in two months, what does four months of me say? Maybe I just don't have the brain for languages. Maybe I should put this time into the placement course instead, something I'm actually good at.
I know, I know, you'll say everyone hits this wall. It doesn't feel like a phase from inside. It feels like a wall with my name on it. Salma, the girl who quit Japanese. Has a ring to it, no?

qa.q: How long has Salma been doing kanji cards?
qa.a: Four months.

qa.q: What was Salma feeling when the newer classmate read the paragraph easily?
qa.a: She felt irritated and jealous, and underneath that scared that she simply lacks the brain for languages.

qa.q: What turning point is open to Salma at this stage?
qa.a: She could compare herself with her own start four months ago instead of a classmate, and ask the teacher how to fix the words she keeps blanking on.

qa.q: How might Hemant see Salma's snapping at everyone lately?
qa.a: Hemant may have felt puzzled or hurt by it, and can now see it as frustration with Japanese rather than anything personal.

grounding: A young adult learner is irritated, compares herself with a faster classmate and seriously considers dropping the skill.

passage:
Monday. Kavitha, nineteen, clung to the edge of the college pool while Jomon, who had started lessons the same week, swam a full length. She laughed it off and tried again. Her legs sank the moment her face went in.
Thursday. The coach moved Jomon up to the deep-end group. Kavitha stayed in the shallow lane with two schoolkids. She kicked the wall hard enough to hurt her toe and went home without showering, jaw tight. "Maybe my body just isn't built for water," she told her roommate.
Saturday. She sat on the bench in her swimsuit for twenty minutes, towel round her shoulders, watching the others. She didn't get in. On her phone she opened the fee page and hovered over the button that said cancel membership. Then Jomon waved from the water. "Coming?"
She didn't answer yet.

qa.q: Where did the coach move Jomon on Thursday?
qa.a: Up to the deep-end group.

qa.q: What does Kavitha kicking the wall suggest about how she felt?
qa.a: She felt angry and humiliated at being left in the shallow lane with schoolkids while Jomon moved up.

qa.q: What turning point is available to Kavitha on Saturday?
qa.a: Instead of cancelling, she could ask the coach exactly why her legs sink and practise only that, one short step at a time.

qa.q: What might Jomon be experiencing when waving Kavitha over?
qa.a: Jomon may not realise how discouraged Kavitha is; the wave is friendly and hopeful that she will join in.

grounding: Across three days a young swimmer grows irritated, compares herself with a faster learner and nearly cancels, the point where many stop.

passage:
Sit, Tanuja, and stop kicking your guitar book under the bed. Let me tell you about Ayesha at nineteen, in the typing institute above the sweet shop in Lucknow. Shorthand. Eighty words a minute to pass, and I was stuck at fifty for two months.
A girl called Nusrat reached eighty in six weeks, and the teacher wrote her speed on the board in red chalk. Mine stayed in plain white. Every morning I looked at that red number and felt my ears burn.
One evening I came home and told my Ammi I was finished. My hand was too slow, my head too stupid. I threw the practice book under the bed, just like you did, and I meant it. I was so angry I couldn't eat.
Next morning my brother fished it out, dusted it and left it on my pillow. He didn't say a word. That small, silly gesture is the only reason I went back for one more week.
So, my girl. Your guitar book. Pick it up.

qa.q: Where was the typing institute Ayesha attended?
qa.a: Above the sweet shop in Lucknow.

qa.q: What was young Ayesha feeling when she threw the practice book under the bed?
qa.a: She felt angry and defeated, sure that her hand was too slow and her head too stupid after comparing herself with Nusrat.

qa.q: What turning point came in the story the next morning?
qa.a: Finding the practice book on her pillow gave Ayesha a quiet nudge to try one more week instead of quitting in anger.

qa.q: How might Ayesha's brother have seen her that evening?
qa.a: He probably saw how hurt and frustrated she was, and chose a silent, kind gesture rather than a lecture.

grounding: An elder recalls being nineteen, irritated at a faster classmate and ready to drop shorthand, the hardest moment to see past.

passage: The pottery studio in Kochi gave each student only twenty minutes on the wheel, and today the power had flickered twice, stopping it mid-spin. Binita's clay slumped sideways for the fourth time. Across the room Jomon, who had joined two weeks after her, lifted a neat, tall cylinder and grinned. Binita's jaw tightened. Six weeks of Saturdays, the long bus ride, clay under her nails for days, and she still couldn't centre a lump. She scraped the ruined clay into the bucket harder than she needed to. On the bus home she opened a message to the studio and typed: "Hi, I think I'll stop after this month, it's not really for me." She read it three times. Her thumb hovered. She didn't send it, and she didn't delete it either.

qa.q: How long did each student get on the wheel?
qa.a: Only twenty minutes.

qa.q: What was Binita feeling when Jomon lifted the tall cylinder?
qa.a: She felt irritated and discouraged, comparing six weeks of struggle with Jomon's quick success.

qa.q: What could help Binita at this turning point?
qa.a: Before sending the message, she could ask the teacher what is going wrong with centring and look at how far she has come.

qa.q: What might Jomon's quick progress feel like from Jomon's side?
qa.a: Jomon may simply be enjoying a good day, unaware that the grin stings Binita.

grounding: Shows a learner irritated by slow progress, comparing herself with a faster classmate and drafting a message to quit at the hardest point.
